sections.h2: Albuquerque at a glance for a seller
sections.html:
New Mexico's biggest city is also the Bernalillo County seat, with 564,559 people in the 2020 census. The Rio Grande cuts through the middle of a basin bounded by the Sandia Mountains on the east and the West Mesa on the west. Houses by the river and houses in the foothills can vary in age, lot type and weather exposure, even in the same ZIP code.

What you owe depends on the parcel rather than the neighborhood label. Neighbors a few blocks apart may fall in different taxing districts or in a special improvement district.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Albuquerque?
sections.html:
Albuquerque addresses get their property tax bill from the Bernalillo County Treasurer, who also collects it, while the county Assessor determines the value. The city itself mails no property tax bill.

Each year the state Department of Finance and Administration sets county rates in September, the Assessor hands the tax roll to the Treasurer by October 1, and bills follow, normally by November 1 or the next business day if that is a weekend.

Visit the Treasurer at 415 Silver Ave SW downtown or call (505) 468-7031. The Assessor shares the building and answers at (505) 222-3700.

Half the bill is due November 10 and the rest April 10. Late fees begin December 10 and May 10, in that order.

DateWhat happens

Confirm any date with the Treasurer before you rely on it, since a deadline that lands on a weekend can shift. For a seller, the November and April payments matter most: ask the title company how the half-year in progress will be divided between you and the buyer, and keep your payment confirmations to prove what was paid.

sections.h2: What happens if tax goes unpaid
sections.html:
A late balance picks up 1% interest each month and a separate 1% monthly penalty. The penalty stops at 5% and has a $5 floor.

Owners remain liable even if no bill arrives. Many bills come back undelivered after the November mailing, mostly because of outdated mailing addresses, so keep the addresses for your Notice of Value and your bill current. Someone who has left an inherited or rented house is the likeliest to miss a bill.

In June the Treasurer mails delinquent notices. An owner who cannot pay everything at once can call the Treasurer to arrange payments, and a monthly plan is available.

sections.h2: Protesting your value and lowering the bill
sections.html:
You have 30 days from the mailing of the Notice of Value to protest the valuation with the Assessor, and several savings programs use the same 30 days. Filing is online through the appeal portal or at 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal talk with a field appraiser comes first. If the value stays disputed, the Protest Valuation Review Board holds a hearing. Someone who misses the window can pay the bill and sue for a refund in the Second Judicial District Court at 400 Lomas Blvd NW, where the county lists a $132 filing fee.

Savings programs worth asking about:

  • Head of Family, which cuts taxable value by $2,000 and applies to one property in the state per household.
  • The veteran exemption, worth up to $10,000 off taxable value, with a state service commission certificate.
  • A value freeze for owners 65 or older with modified gross income of $42,900 or less, or disabled owners at $41,900 or less, which holds the assessed value but not the tax rate.

The state offers no homestead exemption. Taxable value equals one-third of assessed value, and the Head of Family and veteran amounts are subtracted from that taxable figure.

Some Albuquerque subdivisions carry a public improvement district, or PID, which adds a line to the tax bill that pays back bonds for neighborhood infrastructure. The amount per parcel changes from year to year, parcel size and other factors affect it, and a buyer continues the remaining bond payments where the seller left off. An owner may pay a PID off early, and the only exemption on PID payments is the 100% disabled veteran waiver.

If yours is one of them, let the buyer and the title company know early. A cash buyer will fold the remaining balance into the offer, and knowing your payoff figure prevents a surprise at the closing table. The county Assessor keeps a page listing the name and boundary of each district.

They count if the house has ever been rented by the night, since the city requires a permit and enforces it. Albuquerque defines a short-term rental as a dwelling, or part of one, rented for fewer than 29 consecutive days.

The permit needs a business license, a floor plan, proof of insurance of at least $250,000 per unit, and a posted Good Neighbor Agreement. The fee is $120 in the first year and $90 for renewals. Operators must also file a monthly lodgers' tax report by the 25th, even when a platform remits the tax. Operating without a permit can bring fines and a ban on future operation, so a seller with an unpermitted rental past should settle it before listing.

sections.h2: Notices of Value and the seller's timeline
sections.html:
Property is valued as it stands on January 1 and assessed to the owner of record on that date. The Assessor must mail Notices of Value by April 1, and that mailing starts your 30-day clock for protests and exemption applications. A house sold in spring still carries that notice, so tell the buyer about it and decide in the contract who files any protest.

If the property passed to an heir and the deed was never updated, the notice and bill still go to the owner of record. Fix the record before you list so mail reaches a person who can act on it.

Paperwork, not buyers, causes most Albuquerque delays. These come up often:

  • A bill mailed to a former address that is now delinquent.
  • A PID balance that was not known until the title search.
  • An unfinished addition that changes the assessed value, or an unpermitted rental.
  • A deed that never moved into an heir's name after a death.

Whatever route you choose, unpaid tax is paid from the proceeds by the title company at closing. Start by looking up your balance in the Treasurer's online tax search. A cash buyer purchasing as is can absorb many of these problems, but needs the balance figure too.

faqs.q: Does the City of Albuquerque send its own property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. Bernalillo County bills Albuquerque property owners. The Assessor sets the value, the Treasurer mails the bill and collects, and the state sets the rates each September.

faqs.q: When is Albuquerque property tax due?
faqs.a: Half is due November 10 and half is due April 10. Late fees begin December 10 on the first half and May 10 on the second half.

faqs.q: How much are the late fees on Albuquerque property tax?
faqs.a: Interest is 1% of the unpaid tax each month, and the penalty is 1% each month up to 5%, with a $5 minimum penalty.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Albuquerque house if I still owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid tax, with any penalty and interest, is normally paid from the sale proceeds by the title company at closing. Check the exact balance with the Bernalillo County Treasurer first.

faqs.q: Is there a homestead exemption in Albuquerque?
faqs.a: No. New Mexico has no homestead exemption. The Assessor offers Head of Family, which reduces taxable value by $2,000, plus veteran exemptions and a value freeze for qualifying owners.
